pairs.rationale: Both teachings combine lamps, a wedding setting, and readiness for an arriving master or bridegroom. Luke has servants waiting for their master to return from a wedding; Matthew has virgins going to meet the bridegroom, so the roles and journey differ.

The same parable deliberately contrasts the foolish virgins' failure to take oil with the prudent virgins' provision of oil in containers. This links the two opposed preparations within the story, without claiming an independent account.

The prudent virgins' containers of oil directly contrast with the foolish virgins' taking lamps without oil in the preceding description. The comparison concerns the parable's two preparations and supplies no separate allegorical identity for the oil.

Both parables include the master's or bridegroom's delay. Matthew says all the virgins grew sleepy; Luke's slave interprets delay as permission to mistreat others and indulge himself. The differing responses are not equated, and Matthew's sleep is not labelled Luke's misconduct.

Both wedding-related readiness images turn on the awaited figure's arrival and an immediate response by those waiting. Matthew gives a midnight cry to meet the bridegroom; Luke gives the returning master's knock and immediate opening, without the midnight cry.

Both images include a door being shut and late people left outside. Matthew describes the ready virgins entering the wedding feast; Luke describes the householder rising and shutting the door, without this wedding-party scene.
Both depict those left outside appealing to the lord to open the door. Matthew names the late virgins; Luke speaks of hearers standing outside and knocking.

Both warnings express exclusion through denial of recognition. The parable's bridegroom says he does not know the late arrivals; Jesus' earlier judgment warning says He never knew those practicing lawlessness. The different wording and setting remain distinct.
Both commands require keeping watch because the day of the Lord's arrival is unknown; Matthew 25 also names the unknown hour.

Both money parables begin with a departing master or nobleman entrusting resources to slaves. Luke adds the journey to receive a kingdom and a command to do business; the surrounding plots are not made identical.

Both parables describe money being entrusted to slaves before the master's absence. Matthew assigns unequal talents according to ability; Luke names ten minas distributed among ten slaves, with no corresponding ability-based allocation stated in this verse.
Both describe a first slave producing a gain from entrusted money. Matthew's five talents yield five more, while Luke's reported mina yields ten minas; the amounts and rates of increase differ.
Both portray a second slave reporting or achieving a profitable use of entrusted money. Matthew describes two talents gaining two more; Luke's second slave reports a mina making five minas.
Both contrast productive slaves with one who merely preserves the master's money. Matthew's slave buries the silver in the ground; Luke's slave keeps the mina in a cloth.

Both money parables bring the returning master to an accounting with the slaves. Matthew emphasizes a long interval; Luke specifies that the nobleman has received the kingdom and asks about business done.
Both first slaves report the gain on the master's entrusted funds. Matthew's report doubles five talents; Luke's report describes one mina gaining ten minas, so the figures are preserved separately.

Both masters praise the good slave and reward faithfulness in a small trust with greater responsibility. Matthew appoints him over many things and welcomes him into joy; Luke assigns authority over ten cities.
Both accounts include a second profitable slave's report. Matthew reports two talents becoming two more; Luke reports the master's mina making five minas.

Matthew's second slave receives praise for faithfulness over few things and greater responsibility, corresponding to the principle in Luke's praise of the first slave. The slave's position and the reward wording differ; Luke does not reproduce this second-slave speech.
Both unproductive slaves characterize their master as severe and reaping where he did not sow. Matthew also says gathering where he did not scatter; Luke says taking up what he did not lay down.

Both slaves explain their nonproductive preservation of the master's funds through fear of him. Matthew specifies burial in the ground and returning the talent; Luke specifies keeping the mina in a cloth and calls the master severe.

Both masters confront the evil slave with his own description of a severe master who reaps where he did not sow. Luke expressly says judgment comes from the slave's own mouth; Matthew additionally calls him idle.
Both masters ask why the money was not placed on deposit so it could be recovered with interest at the return.
Both direct that the unproductive slave's entrusted money be taken and given to the one who has ten. Matthew uses talents and Luke minas; the denominations are not equated.
Both conclude the money-distribution judgment with more being given to the one who has and even the existing possession taken from the one who does not have. Matthew additionally mentions abundance.

Both warnings describe exclusion into outer darkness accompanied by weeping and grinding of teeth. Matthew 25 applies it to the useless slave in the money parable; Matthew 8 uses it in the warning about sons of the kingdom.
Both describe the Son of Man coming in glory with angels for judgment. Matthew 25 adds His sitting on the throne of glory; Matthew 16 explicitly says He will repay each person according to conduct.

The Son of Man's sheep-and-goats separation recalls the Lord's promised distinction among sheep, rams, and male goats in Ezekiel. Matthew gathers all nations, while Ezekiel addresses the flock; the groups and scope are not silently equated.

Both associate the kingdom's gift with the Father. Matthew's King invites the blessed to inherit the kingdom prepared from the world's foundation; Luke assures the little flock that the Father was pleased to give them the kingdom.

Both commend feeding hungry people and welcoming people in need. Isaiah commands sharing bread and bringing homeless poor people into one's house; Matthew describes feeding the hungry King and welcoming Him as a stranger. Isaiah's verse does not include Matthew's act of giving drink.

Matthew commends coming to the imprisoned and caring for the afflicted; Hebrews commands remembering prisoners as fellow prisoners and those being mistreated. The link concerns embodied solidarity with prisoners, without making Hebrews repeat all the clothing and sickness details.

The King identifies kindness toward the least of His brothers with kindness toward Himself; Proverbs describes mercy to the poor as lending to God. Both relate aid to other people to a divine recipient or repayment, without assuming the two passages define their human beneficiaries identically.

Both judgment scenes describe the condemned being consigned to fire. Matthew 25 calls it eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels; Matthew 13 describes a furnace of fire with weeping and grinding of teeth, without that statement about its preparation.

Both expose failure to supply food to a person in bodily need. James contrasts well-wishing with withholding what the body requires; Matthew's judgment accusation specifies hunger and thirst, while James's example names food and clothing rather than drink.

Matthew condemns withholding welcome from a stranger and clothing from the naked; Isaiah commands bringing homeless poor people into one's house and clothing the naked. This compares corresponding acts and omissions without treating all of Matthew's sickness and prison details as present in Isaiah.

The King repeats the same scene's identification of treatment of the least with treatment of Himself, now in the negative. The earlier positive verdict supplies the deliberate contrast between service and failure to serve; this is an internal literary comparison.

Both contrast enduring favorable and unfavorable outcomes: Matthew names eternal life and eternal punishment, while this supplied Daniel text names everlasting life, reproach, dispersion, and everlasting shame. Daniel explicitly frames the contrast through sleepers arising; Matthew's verse concludes the nations' judgment.

Both place the Passover two days away as the passion narrative begins. Matthew gives Jesus' prediction of being handed over for crucifixion; Mark states the date while describing the authorities' plan to seize and kill Him.

Both introduce chief-priestly opposition planning Jesus' arrest and death near Passover. Matthew specifies the elders' meeting in Caiaphas's courtyard; Mark names scribes and does not supply the courtyard or high priest's name in this verse.
Both describe the authorities seeking to seize Jesus by deceit and kill Him.
Both record the decision to avoid the feast because of the risk of a disturbance among the people.
Both place the anointing meal in Bethany at the house of Simon the leper; Mark includes the anointing itself in the same verse.
Both describe a woman pouring expensive perfume from an alabaster container onto Jesus' head while He reclines. Mark additionally names pure nard and says the jar was broken.
Both record indignation and the question why the perfume was wasted. Matthew identifies the disciples, while Mark describes some people being indignant without naming them in this verse.

Both argue that the perfume could have been sold and the money given to the poor. Mark specifies more than three hundred denarii and also describes harsh scolding; Matthew states only a large sale value.
Both have Jesus challenge the mistreatment of the woman and call her action toward Him a good work.
Both contrast the continuing presence of poor people with Jesus' limited presence among the hearers. Mark additionally says they can do good to the poor whenever they wish.
Both interpret the woman's anointing of Jesus' body as preparation for burial; Mark also says she did what she could.
Both promise that wherever the gospel is proclaimed throughout the world the woman's deed will be recounted in remembrance of her.
Both identify Judas Iscariot as one of the Twelve and describe his approach to the chief priests to hand Jesus over.

Both connect Judas's betrayal arrangement with payment in silver. Matthew supplies his question and thirty silver coins; Mark records the priests' pleasure and promise of silver money without specifying thirty.
Both describe Judas seeking a suitable opportunity to hand Jesus over after the payment arrangement.
Both place the disciples' question about preparing Jesus' Passover meal on the first day of Unleavened Bread. Mark additionally explains it as the day of sacrificing the Passover.

Both direct disciples into the city to arrange a place for Jesus to eat the Passover with them, using a message from the Teacher. Mark supplies the water-jar bearer and furnished upper room; Matthew supplies the appointed time's nearness and addresses a certain man without those additional directions.
Both describe the disciples following Jesus' directions and preparing the Passover; Mark also states that they found things as He had said.
Both place Jesus with the Twelve in the evening meal scene; Mark's two verses describe His arrival and the ensuing reclining and eating.
Both record Jesus' announcement during the meal that one of His companions will hand Him over. Mark additionally emphasizes that the betrayer is eating with Him.
Both describe the disciples' grief and their individual questions whether they are the betrayer. Matthew gives their address Lord; Mark's cited wording does not include that address.
Both identify the betrayer through sharing the dipping dish with Jesus. Matthew specifies the hand; Mark additionally calls him one of the Twelve.
Both juxtapose the Son of Man's scriptural course with a woe on His betrayer and the statement that it would have been good for that man not to have been born.

Matthew singles out Judas asking whether he is the betrayer, corresponding to Mark's report of the companions asking that question one by one. Matthew gives Judas's address Rabbi and Jesus' reply You have said it; Mark's cited verse does not single out Judas or give that reply.
Both describe Jesus taking, blessing, breaking, and giving bread while identifying it as His body. Matthew additionally includes the command eat.
Both describe Jesus taking a cup, giving thanks, and giving it to the disciples. Matthew gives the instruction that all should drink; Mark reports that they all drank.
Both identify the cup with Jesus' blood of the covenant poured out for many. Matthew adds for forgiveness of sins, a clause absent from this supplied verse in Mark.
Both promise no further drinking of the fruit of the vine until drinking it new in the kingdom. Matthew says with you in My Father's kingdom; Mark says in God's kingdom.
Both describe singing a hymn before going out to the Mount of Olives.
Both predict the disciples' stumbling and cite the shepherd being struck and the sheep scattered. Matthew additionally specifies this night and the sheep of the flock.
Both promise that after being raised Jesus will go ahead of the disciples to Galilee.
Both record Peter claiming that he will not stumble even if all the others do.
Both predict Peter's three denials that night before the rooster's crowing. Mark explicitly says before a rooster crows twice, whereas Matthew does not include twice.
Both record Peter insisting he will not deny Jesus even if he must die with Him, and both say the other disciples make the same claim.
Both place Jesus and the disciples at Gethsemane and give His instruction to sit while He prays.
Both describe Jesus taking Peter with the two companions and becoming distressed. Matthew identifies the others as Zebedee's two sons; Mark names James and John.
Both describe Jesus' soul as deeply grieved to death and His request that the companions remain and keep watch.

Both describe Jesus moving away, falling to the ground, and praying that the cup or hour pass while submitting His will to the Father's. Matthew specifies falling on His face; Mark records the address Abba and the Father's ability to do all things.
Both have Jesus return to sleeping disciples and challenge Peter about failing to keep watch for one hour. Mark addresses him as Simon.
Both require watchfulness and prayer against entering temptation and contrast the willing spirit with weak flesh.

Both describe Jesus going away to pray again. Matthew supplies the second prayer's wording about drinking the cup and the Father's will; Mark says He repeated the same word without reproducing that second prayer's wording.
Both describe Jesus again finding the disciples asleep because their eyes were heavy; Mark adds that they did not know how to answer Him.

Both narratives describe repeated prayer and repeated visits to the sleeping disciples. Matthew expressly states a third prayer with the same words; Mark records repeated prayer and then a third return, without explicitly narrating a distinct third prayer in this cited passage.
Both have Jesus tell the disciples to sleep and rest as the hour arrives and the Son of Man is handed over into sinners' hands.
Both record Jesus' summons to rise and go because the betrayer has drawn near.
Both introduce Judas as one of the Twelve arriving while Jesus still speaks, accompanied by an armed crowd sent by the religious authorities. Mark additionally names scribes among those authorities.
Both describe Judas arranging a kiss as the sign identifying whom the armed party should seize; Mark also directs them to lead Him away securely.
Both narrate Judas approaching, addressing Jesus as Rabbi, and kissing Him. Matthew additionally gives the greeting.

Both narrate the party laying hands on Jesus and seizing Him. Matthew additionally records Jesus' address to Judas as friend and His instruction concerning what Judas came for; Mark's cited verse gives only the arrest.
Both describe someone near Jesus drawing a sword and cutting off the high priest's slave's ear. Neither of these two supplied verses names the swordsman.

Both have Jesus command that the sword be put away during the arrest. Matthew adds the warning about sword-users perishing by the sword; John addresses Peter and gives the Father's cup as the reason for submission.

Jesus speaks of help His Father could provide in overwhelming numbers; Elisha assures his attendant of more numerous help and prays for his eyes to see the fiery horses and chariot around him. The comparison concerns divine protective resources; Kings does not name those visible figures angels or number them as twelve legions, and Matthew does not say Jesus summoned them.

Jesus' arrest saying asks how the Scriptures could otherwise be fulfilled; His later explanation in Luke describes the Christ's necessary suffering and interprets the Scriptures about Himself. The settings are before the passion and after the resurrection respectively.
Both contrast the armed arrest as though against a robber with Jesus' prior public teaching in the temple when He was not seized.
Both connect the arrest with fulfillment of Scripture and then describe all the disciples leaving and fleeing. Matthew expressly calls them the Scriptures of the prophets.
Both describe Jesus being taken to the high priest, where the scribes and elders assemble. Matthew names Caiaphas; Mark's cited verse leaves the high priest unnamed and also lists chief priests.
Both have Peter follow at a distance into the high priest's courtyard and sit with the attendants. Matthew says he wanted to see the outcome; Mark describes warming at the firelight.
Both describe the chief priests and council seeking testimony to put Jesus to death. Matthew calls the sought testimony false; Mark's next verse explains the false witnesses and their disagreement.
Both describe unsuccessful false testimony followed by accusers standing forward. Matthew specifically says two finally came; Mark describes some standing up without assigning that number here.

Both witnesses allege that Jesus spoke of destroying the sanctuary and rebuilding in three days. Matthew's accusation says I can destroy God's sanctuary; Mark's says I will destroy the hand-made sanctuary and build another not made by hands. The accusation wordings are preserved separately.
Both describe the high priest rising and challenging Jesus to answer the testimony against Him.

Both describe Jesus' silence followed by the high priest's question whether He is the Christ and divine Son. Matthew adjures Him by the living God and says Son of God; Mark says Son of the Blessed One.
Both answer with the Son of Man seated at the right of the Power and coming with heaven's clouds. Matthew begins You have said it; Mark begins I am, so the opening responses are not harmonized.
Both describe the high priest tearing his garments, dismissing the need for further witnesses, and declaring that the hearers have heard blasphemy.
Both give the council's resulting judgment that Jesus deserves death.
Both describe spitting, fist blows, and slaps during the abuse. Mark additionally describes covering His face; that detail is not supplied in Matthew's cited verse.
Both mock Jesus with the command to prophesy who struck Him. Luke explicitly describes blindfolding, a detail not given in Matthew's supplied verse.
Both place Peter in the courtyard and describe a female servant identifying him with Jesus. Matthew calls Jesus the Galilean; Mark calls Him the Nazarene and mentions Peter warming himself.
Both give Peter's denial through claiming not to know or understand what the woman says. Mark additionally describes his movement outside and an initial rooster crow.

Both have a female servant identify Peter to people standing nearby after his movement outward. Matthew calls her another girl and refers to Jesus the Nazarene; Mark refers back to the female slave without introducing another one here.
Both report Peter denying the identification again. Matthew explicitly adds an oath and denial of knowing the Man; Mark's cited verse gives the renewed denial without that oath.

Both have the bystanders renew the identification of Peter through his Galilean association. Matthew specifies recognition through his speech; Mark explicitly calls him Galilean without mentioning an accent here.
Both describe Peter invoking curses and swearing he does not know the Man, followed by a rooster crow. Mark calls this the second crow, while Matthew does not record an earlier crow in this scene.
Both have the rooster remind Peter of Jesus' prediction and lead to weeping. Matthew's remembered prediction lacks Mark's twice for the crow, and Matthew describes going outside to weep bitterly.
